SOURCE: "Mixed Precision Training", Micikevicius, Narang, Alben, Diamos, Elsen, Garcia, Ginsburg, Houston, Kuchaiev, Venkatesh, Wu (Baidu Research + NVIDIA). ICLR 2018 conference paper, arXiv:1710.03740v3 (15 Feb 2018). Micikevicius and Narang are marked equal contribution. The extracted header lists the Baidu authors (Narang, Diamos, Elsen) first, but citing as "Micikevicius et al." is standard.

COVERAGE: 34,463 of 34,463 chars, which is all 12 of 12 pages. Pages 1-9 are the body. Pages 10-12 are references, which I skimmed for origins. There is no appendix. File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/02-rag-retrieval/sources/micikevicius-2017-mixed-precision-training.pdf. The PDF sits under 02-rag-retrieval/sources even though the target note is in 01-llm-fundamentals.

KEY POINT FOR THE TARGET NOTE: the paper does NOT support the "16 bytes per parameter" figure. It never counts bytes per parameter, never counts optimizer state, and never mentions Adam momentum or variance. Its only memory accounting is about weights (p3): "maintaining an additional copy of weights increases the memory requirements for the weights by 50% compared with single precision training". It says overall memory "is roughly halved" because activations dominate. The 2+2+12 = 16-byte breakdown matches the accounting in ZeRO (arXiv:1910.02054), which the note already cites in the next sentence. I did not read ZeRO, so I cannot confirm that it states it. Cite Micikevicius for the method (fp32 master weights, loss scaling, fp32 accumulation), not for the byte count.

CLAIMS
- claim: The method has three techniques. (1) Keep an FP32 master copy of the weights, updated each optimizer step and rounded to FP16 for the forward and backward passes. (2) Scale the loss so small gradients are not lost. (3) Do FP16 arithmetic that accumulates into FP32 and converts back to FP16 before writing to memory.
  number: none
  setup: general method. Weights, activations and gradients are stored in IEEE FP16.
  quote: "Firstly, we recommend maintaining a single-precision copy of weights that accumulates the gradients after each optimizer step (this copy is rounded to half-precision for the forward- and back-propagation). Secondly, we propose loss-scaling to preserve gradient values with small magnitudes. Thirdly, we use half-precision arithmetic that accumulates into single-precision outputs, which are converted to half-precision before storing to memory."
  where: p1, abstract
- claim: Memory is about halved overall, even though the master copy raises weight memory by 50%, because activations dominate training memory and are stored in FP16.
  number: 50% more weight memory; overall "roughly halved"
  setup: an argument, not measured. No byte-level or optimizer-state accounting.
  quote: "Even though maintaining an additional copy of weights increases the memory requirements for the weights by 50% compared with single precision training, impact on overall memory usage is much smaller. For training memory consumption is dominated by activations ... the overall memory consumption for training deep neural networks is roughly halved."
  where: p3, sec 3.1
- claim: Without FP32 master weights, a speech model loses 80% relative accuracy, because about 5% of weight gradients fall below FP16's smallest value (2^-24) and become zero.
  number: 80% relative accuracy loss; ~5% of gradients; 2^-24
  setup: Mandarin DeepSpeech 2 speech model, ~800 h of speech, 20 epochs, pseudo-FP16 run
  quote: "updating FP16 weights results in 80% relative accuracy loss." / "any value whose magnitude is smaller than 2−24 becomes zero in FP16. We can see in Figure 2b that approximately 5% of weight gradient values have exponents smaller than−24."
  where: p3, sec 3.1
- claim: An update is lost when the weight is more than 2048 times larger than the update, because FP16 has 10 mantissa bits.
  number: 2048
  setup: a property of the FP16 number format
  quote: "This can happen when the magnitude of a normalized weight value is at least 2048 times larger that of the weight update. Since FP16 has 10 bits of mantissa"
  where: p3
- claim: Loss scaling multiplies the loss before backpropagation, so the chain rule scales every gradient by the same amount. Gradients are unscaled before clipping and the weight update. The scale factor must keep the largest gradient times the factor below 65,504. On overflow, the step can be skipped.
  number: scale factors 8 to 32K; FP16 maximum 65,504
  setup: many networks needed no scaling at all
  quote: "We trained a variety of networks with scaling factors ranging from 8 to 32K (many networks did not require a scaling factor)." / "its product with the maximum absolute gradient value is below 65,504 (the maximum value representable in FP16)." / "One option is to skip the weight update when an overflow is detected"
  where: p4-5, sec 3.2
- claim: Multibox SSD diverges without loss scaling and matches FP32 with a factor of 8. Faster R-CNN dips slightly without scaling.
  number: SSD 76.9% baseline mAP vs diverges vs 77.1%; Faster R-CNN 69.1 / 68.6 / 69.7
  setup: VGG-16 backbone, Pascal VOC 2007 test set
  quote: "Faster R-CNN 69.1% 68.6% 69.7%" / "Multibox SSD 76.9% diverges 77.1%" / "loss-scaling factor of 8 recovers the relevant gradient values"
  where: p6, Table 2
- claim: Six ImageNet CNNs match FP32 top-1 accuracy with the same hyperparameters and no loss scaling.
  number: e.g. ResNet50 75.92% vs 76.04%; AlexNet 56.77 vs 56.93; Inception v3 73.85 vs 74.13
  setup: ILSVRC12 validation set, single crop. Caffe with Volta TensorOps; PyTorch for ResNet50. Single runs.
  quote: "Resnet50 75.92% 76.04%" / "Loss-scaling technique was not required for successful mixed precision training of these networks."
  where: p6, Table 1
- claim: The language model needs loss scaling. Without it, FP16 diverges after 300K iterations. A factor of 128 matches FP32.
  number: 128; 300K iterations
  setup: bigLSTM on 1B Word, 2x8192 LSTM, 793K vocab, Adagrad, 50 epochs, batch 1024 across 4 GPUs
  quote: "Without loss scaling the training perplexity curve for FP16 training diverges, compared with the FP32 training, after 300K iterations. Scaling factor of 128 recovers all the relevant gradient values"
  where: p7, sec 4.5
- claim: The speech models came out slightly better in pseudo-FP16 than in FP32. The authors suggest FP16 may act as a regularizer.
  number: CER English 2.20 vs 1.99; Mandarin 15.82 vs 15.01
  setup: DeepSpeech 2, 115M params (English, 6000 h) and 215M params (Mandarin, 2600 h), Nesterov SGD, 20 epochs. FP16 storage only, emulated on Maxwell GPUs.
  quote: "English 2.20 1.99" / "Mandarin 15.82 15.01" / "Pseudo FP16 results are roughly 5 to 10% better than the baseline."
  where: p7, Table 3
- claim: Large reductions such as batch-norm statistics and softmax should be done in FP32. Point-wise operations can use either precision.
  number: none
  setup: implementation guidance
  quote: "Large reductions (sums across elements of a vector) should be carried out in FP32."
  where: p5, sec 3.3
- claim: Only operation-level speedups are reported, not end-to-end training speedups.
  number: 2-6x
  setup: DeepBench on Volta, for operations limited by memory or arithmetic bandwidth
  quote: "DNN operations benchmarked with DeepBench on Volta GPU see 2-6x speedups compared to FP32 implementations if they are limited by memory or arithmetic bandwidth."
  where: p8, sec 5
- claim: The hardware motivation is that half-precision math runs 2-8x faster than single precision on recent GPUs.
  number: 2x to 8x
  setup: GPUs of 2017
  quote: "half-precision math throughput in recent GPUs is 2 × to 8× higher than for single-precision."
  where: p1

LIMITS
- No bytes-per-parameter accounting and no optimizer-state memory. Adam appears only as the DCGAN optimizer (p8). The other runs use SGD, Nesterov SGD or Adagrad.
- No bf16. The only format covered is IEEE FP16.
- No LLM-scale or Transformer runs. The largest model is 215M parameters, the Mandarin speech model. The language model is an LSTM, and translation uses 3- or 5-layer LSTMs.
- Dynamic loss scaling is only proposed as future work (p9): "Loss-scaling factor could be dynamically increased or decreased by inspecting the weight gradients for overflow". The experiments use constant factors.
- No end-to-end wall-clock speedups. The authors write: "Full network training and inference speedups depend on library and framework optimizations ... experiments in this paper were carried out with early versions".
- Results are single runs, apart from the three FP32 reference curves in Figure 4. The authors concede "There was a noticeable variation in accuracy of different training sessions with the same settings."
- Translation results appear only as curves, with no BLEU. The GAN result is qualitative only ("Qualitatively the outputs ... appear comparable").
- The speech results are emulated (FP16 storage only, on Maxwell), not run on Volta Tensor Cores.
- The claim of "no hyper-parameter changes" sits alongside a loss-scale factor that still has to be chosen per model.
- Dated: hardware is Volta-era. Text-to-speech and reinforcement learning are listed as future work.

BUILDS ON: Courbariaux et al. (2015), BinaryConnect; Hubara et al. (2016a, 2016b), binarized and quantized networks; Rastegari et al. (2016), XNOR-Net; Zhou et al. (2016), DoReFa-Net; Mishra et al. (2017), WRPN; Gupta et al. (2015), 16-bit fixed point on MNIST and CIFAR-10; He et al. (2016c) and Ott et al. (2016), quantized RNNs; NVIDIA (2017), V100 Tensor Cores. The paper's stated contrast is that prior work kept gradients in FP32 or lost accuracy.

CODE: none in the paper.

FIGURES
- Fig 1, p3, "Mixed precision training iteration for a layer." Best single figure: it shows the FP32 master copy, the FP16 forward and backward passes, and the update loop in one diagram.
- Fig 3, p4, histogram of SSD activation gradients against the FP16 representable range ("67% of values are zero"). It shows at a glance why loss scaling works: shifting the gradients right moves them into the usable range.
- Fig 2a/2b, p4, Mandarin training curves with and without the master copy, plus a histogram of weight-gradient exponents. Shows that the master weights are necessary.
- Fig 5, p8, bigLSTM perplexity with and without loss scaling. Shows the divergence.
- Fig 4, p7, translation perplexity with three FP32 reference runs (useful for seeing run-to-run variance). Fig 6, p8, DCGAN faces. Both are low priority.

PROBLEMS: Text extraction was clean. Small faults only: ligatures (ﬁ, ﬂ), "V olta" split into two words, and a typo in the source ("experiemnts"). Some section headings were split ("I NTRODUCTION"). There were no embedded instructions.
